en: My shriveled hooves
Shall spread as broad as a great cauldron.
I will stretch my mouth against the reins
Until I deliver your punishment;
I will bend my body from head to foot,
And make the woman who asked for the horse
Despair of her fly-sized life.
I will truly open your eyes,
Carry you off and subdue you,
And kill you.
I will run on and gouge you.”
Kyyaz returned to his throne.
At that moment Aichürök
Lashed the cloud-swift bay horse
Wildly from side to side,
Digging in her heels left and right,
And set out upon the road.
The ground crumbled beneath his tracks,
And he thundered faster as he went,
His soles pounding upon the earth,
The bit of black steel
Clanging in his throat.
Though only a beast, the great bay horse
Raced against the flying birds;
The pale reins, knotted at the grip,
Stretched taut between both hands
Of the terrified woman,
As she struggled with the bit
Of the plunging bay horse.
Wiser than a mere beast, Tootoru thought:
“If I do not twist my neck like a stag,
Suddenly bolt away
And dash her into a pit,
Until she is utterly smashed to pieces!
If I do not pour out your blood by the flaskful
And truly drain your strength,
You wicked daughter of Akun,
If I do not tear out your life!
If I do not cast you down and spill
Your black blood by the flaskful!
She wears a coat befitting a hero,
And mounts a mighty horse as though she were one.
The ravine is deep, the cliff sheer,
You accursed, blazing wretch,
You brazen woman,
Who deceived brave Kyyaz,
You surpassingly cunning infidel—
I shall wrench my neck like a stag.
If a cliff a spear’s height rises,
I shall leap without turning aside.
I shall dash her brains out on the stones,
He raced along the rugged slope.
The bay horse flew at a gallop,
And Aichürök upon his back
Despaired of her fragile life.
The white reins, knotted short,
Strained rigid in her hands when pulled.
The hostility of the masterless brute
Now plainly revealed itself.
He thundered onward like a flying cloud,
And wherever his hooves struck, the black earth
Burst apart on every side.
Truly, Chürök’s
Fragile soul cried out in terror.
He bolted wildly, snorting,
And raced headlong, bent on mischief;
That great bay horse, a veritable scourge,
Flew like a cloud.
“If I turn him aside, I am dead;
In this relentless place
I have seen what Tootoru can do,”
Thought Chürök, her soul nearly departing.
Tootoru bolted away,
Bringing cruel havoc;
He ran without swerving,
For Tootoru was a beast indeed,
While Aichürök upon his back
Despaired of her precious life.
Er Kyyaz’s bay horse Tootoru
Plainly showed his malice.
“If this bay horse has his way,
He will carry me into a fire-pit
That scorches the feet, and hurl me in;
He will carry me into a misery
No one can cross and escape;
He will carry me into a snare
From which no trapped soul can emerge;
He will carry me where the clear sky is veiled,
Into the enemy host, and cast me down.”
The noble but ill-fated woman
Thought long and hard:
“Those bulging eyes of yours—
I shall kill you myself!
If I cannot settle your account,
You accursed, demon-ridden beast,
If I cannot beat the frenzy out of you,
And dash your hide against the stones!
I shall subdue this woman,
Carry her off, and take her.
I shall bend the back and neck
Of this woman who thinks herself so strong;
I shall bring her untimely death,
And utterly thwart all her schemes;
I shall plunge her into chaos
And take my vengeance at last!”
So thinking, the charger
Lowered his head to the ground
And lengthened his stride beyond all measure.
His soles thundered upon the earth,
The bit of black steel
Clanged deep in his throat;
His mane and tail streamed wide,
His forelegs stabbed the ground,
His forelock parted across his brow,
And in the roaring brute
The marks of a true charger appeared.
His ribs drew taut,
His hooves bit into the ground,
His spine jutted out,
And his great bones bulged
As he raced onward thus.
He meant to twist his neck like a stag,
Swerve toward a pit as deep as a man is tall,
And cast himself into it,
To bring outright death
Upon moon-faced Chürök,
To find some means to destroy her
And wreak his fury at last.
Tootoru, wiser than a mere beast,
Struck all four hooves against the ground,
While his thick, armful of a tail
Became a horse lower than a swine.
She bound his forelegs and hindlegs fast,
And brought humiliation upon the bay horse.
She made that bay horse a nag,
A stunted thing unable to keep pace with sheep;
Binding his forelegs, she disgraced him,
Binding his hindlegs, she made him slow as an ox.
Then Aichürök
Dealt treacherously with the wicked bay horse:
She lashed him hard from either side,
And drove her heels into him left and right.
Tireless Chürök travelled on,
Covering a great distance without sparing the horse.
God granted her desire:
That day she saw her son and brother-in-law
Alive and unharmed.
At twilight, as the sun went down
And the foremost of the people lay in pairs,
At a spur where the mountain ended,
Upon a bare projecting knoll,
Aichürök arrived without stopping
At a spreading tree where the people rested.
From the restless bay horse
She removed the saddle and left him bare,
Hobbled and tethered him securely,
Then used the white saddle-frame as her pillow,
Lying with her head toward the qibla.
She placed the leather saddlecloth and blue pad
Beneath her hip as bedding,
And that day the woman Aichürök
Fell into a mighty sleep.
Propping herself on one elbow, she slept,
Dozed awhile and rested peacefully,
Lay on her side and eased her soul,
And slept until she was satisfied.
When dawn arrived,
She awoke with a start,
Turned onto her right side,
Recalled Er Kyyaz with alarm,
And saddled Tootoru.
She resolved to settle the score,
And to perform a wonder
Upon the beastly charger Tootoru.
The valiant woman Aichürök
Was a being of sacred power:
Her tongue bore a mystic seal,
Her curses never missed their mark,
And her spells were never cast in vain.
When Chürök was still a maiden,
She had recited wondrous incantations;
Those who saw her power recoiled,
And those who saw her deeds marvelled.
No living soul knew all that she knew,
And she never went without reciting spells.
She was a mighty sorceress and rain-maker—
Behold this art possessed
By the unfortunate daughter of Akun!
Upon the formidable bay charger,
Upon each moving hoof,
She cast a chilling spell,
And did this marvel
To the beast that had bolted with her.
Before one could cry, “Turn this way or that,”
In the blink of an eye,
She made the powerful bay horse
Unable to keep pace with a sheep.
That peerless charger, the bay horse,
She made unable to keep pace with an ox.
He could no longer trot straight,
Nor recover his former strength;
He could not even keep pace with sheep.
The great bay horse had bolted away,
Intent on subduing Aichürök,
But majestic Aichürök
Bound the matchless charger’s fleetness
And reduced him to an ox.
He could no longer trot as before,
Nor recover his former strength;
An hour after he had bolted,
His heel was scarcely a handspan—
A descendant of Er Kutubiy,
The very apple of the hero’s eye,
The son of the warrior Muraapy,
Black Giant, who had come as a captive,
Had remained behind seeking a remedy
And had found Kyzylsart.
This poor heir of Muraapy
Had joined what was severed
And gathered what was scattered.
Across the four corners of the world
He had galloped in every direction,
And Black Giant had found and brought
The great healer Kyzylsart.
God had granted their wish!
When he came and looked inside the tent,
The heart of Chürök, the hero’s daughter,
Was overwhelmed with emotion,
For Kyzylsart, friend of the grey-maned hero,
Appeared there in the tent.
When he saw Aichürök,
His heart was overcome,
And seeing his friend’s wife, Kyzylsart
Shed tears from his eyes:
“My dear kinswoman Aichürök,
Parted from your noble lord,
You have wandered homeless and forlorn,
Wrapping yourself as though to bind your shroud,
Yet swallowing hard as though you would never die;
You became a captured soul,
A miserable prisoner of Kyyaz,
Yearning for just one glimpse
Of the countless Kyrgyz clans.
While the sea-like grey-maned hero lived,
He was an encircling net of iron;
But when that sea-like hero passed away,
You became Kyyaz’s despised spoil.
You have faded pale as white feather grass,
Parted from your noble lord,
And become Kyyaz’s captive prize.”
The bloom had fallen from her face;
Tormented by thoughts of her brother-in-law Choro and Seytek,
The woman trembled with grief.
She crossed a rise curved like a saddle’s back,
Bending forward as she passed over it,
Then entered the broad valley
